title: Does SEO Still Matter With AI Search? What Pacific Northwest Businesses Should Consider
metaTitle: Does SEO Still Matter With AI Search? | YB Marketing
metaDescription: AI is changing how customers search, but SEO still matters. Learn how Pacific Northwest businesses can adapt their search strategy for Google and AI platforms.
contentHtml:
The way people search for businesses and information is becoming more fragmented. Google remains a primary source of discovery, particularly for high-intent and local searches, but customers are increasingly moving between traditional search results, map listings, AI-generated answers, social platforms, Reddit, YouTube, and other sources before making a decision.

For businesses, this does not make SEO less important. It changes what a strong search strategy needs to accomplish.

For many years, SEO performance was evaluated largely through rankings, organic traffic, and conversions. Those metrics remain important, particularly when someone is actively searching for a product or service. At the same time, businesses now need to consider whether search engines and AI systems can clearly understand who they are, what they specialize in, where they operate, and why their information should be considered credible.

Search Behavior Depends on the Business

One of the reasons broad predictions about the death of SEO are not particularly useful is that search behavior varies significantly by industry and intent.

Consider an HVAC contractor serving Yakima and the Tri-Cities. A homeowner with a failed air conditioner is still likely to search Google, review local results, compare businesses, and call a provider. Map visibility, reviews, service pages, and traditional organic rankings can directly influence that decision.

A Seattle technology company selling a complex B2B product may have a very different customer journey. Its prospects might use Google, ChatGPT, industry websites, comparison articles, Reddit discussions, and several visits to the company's website before ever contacting sales.

Both companies need search visibility, but they do not need identical strategies.

For that reason, we believe businesses should begin by understanding how their customers research a purchase rather than treating AI search as a standalone tactic that every company must approach in the same way.

Traditional SEO Still Matters for Commercial Intent

AI-generated answers are particularly well suited to informational questions. Someone searching for the expected lifespan of a heat pump may receive a useful answer without visiting a website at all.

A search for heat pump repair Yakima, however, carries a different type of intent. The person is looking for a company that can perform the work. That creates a stronger reason to view service pages, reviews, project information, credentials, and contact details. A focused SEO strategy still captures that high-intent demand.

This distinction is important because it helps businesses determine where traditional rankings continue to have the greatest commercial value. Local services, professional services, complex purchases, and searches involving provider comparisons still create substantial opportunities for organic search.

AI Makes Subject Depth More Important

Where AI changes the equation most significantly is in how businesses establish expertise online.

A website that contains a homepage, a short services page, an about page, and a contact page provides relatively little context about the company's knowledge. A more developed website can explain individual services, answer customer questions, document projects, discuss processes, address regional considerations, and connect related subjects through a clear content structure.

For a commercial landscaping company in Central Washington, that might include meaningful information about irrigation, water management, seasonal maintenance, plant selection, landscape construction, drainage, and regional growing conditions. For an industrial contractor, it might involve technical processes, equipment, safety requirements, applications, and project planning.

That depth benefits traditional SEO because search engines can better understand the site's subject matter. It also creates more useful source material for AI search visibility and generative answer systems. For a practical guide on that shift, see how to show up in ChatGPT and AI search.

Regional Expertise Can Be a Competitive Advantage

Pacific Northwest businesses often have expertise that is difficult for national content publishers to reproduce well. Climate, regulations, geography, seasonality, customer expectations, and service-area logistics can all influence how a company performs its work.

The opportunity is not to repeatedly insert Washington or a city name into otherwise generic content. It is to explain where regional conditions materially affect the recommendation.

A landscaping company in Central Washington may have meaningful insight into irrigation and plant selection in a dry climate. A roofing company in Western Washington may encounter different weather-related concerns. A contractor serving Yakima, Ellensburg, and the Tri-Cities may have different service-area considerations than a company operating within a dense Seattle metro area.

When that expertise is relevant, it should appear naturally throughout the website.

What We Think Businesses Should Focus On

We are paying more attention to whether websites establish clear topical depth, strong internal relationships between pages, useful first-party information, consistent business details, and credible third-party references. We are also looking more closely at visibility that may occur without a traditional website visit, including patterns described in our article on zero-click local marketing in Washington.

That does not mean replacing established SEO practices with a new checklist labeled AI SEO. Technical quality, crawlability, indexing, site architecture, internal linking, local optimization, useful content, backlinks, and conversion tracking all remain important. When you evaluate performance, start with what actually moves leads in an SEO audit mindset rather than vanity metrics alone.

The difference is that search visibility now extends beyond a familiar list of ten organic results.

Summary

AI is changing search behavior, but it does not eliminate the need for businesses to be discoverable, understandable, and credible online. The strongest approach is not to choose between SEO and AI search. It is to build a digital presence that works across both.

Businesses that clearly explain their services, demonstrate subject expertise, provide useful regional information, maintain strong technical foundations, and earn legitimate recognition across the web are better positioned regardless of how individual search platforms continue to evolve.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is SEO becoming less important because of ChatGPT?

Not necessarily. Traditional search remains particularly valuable for local, commercial, and transactional searches. AI creates additional discovery paths, but it does not eliminate existing ones.

Should a local business optimize specifically for AI search?

AI visibility should be considered alongside traditional SEO rather than treated as a completely separate discipline. Many of the fundamentals overlap.

Does regional content help with SEO?

It can, particularly when location genuinely affects the service. Regional information should provide useful context rather than simply repeat city names.

Can AI search traffic be tracked?

Some referral traffic from AI platforms can be identified in analytics. However, not every AI interaction results in a website visit, which is why broader visibility and brand signals may also become important.

title: How Can a Pacific Northwest Business Show Up in ChatGPT and AI Search?
metaTitle: How Can Your Business Show Up in AI Search?
metaDescription: Learn how Pacific Northwest businesses can strengthen visibility in ChatGPT and AI search through clearer content, authority, local relevance, and third-party signals.
contentHtml:
Businesses are increasingly asking how they can appear in ChatGPT, Google's AI-generated search experiences, and other AI platforms. The question is reasonable, particularly as customers begin using these tools to research companies, compare options, and understand unfamiliar services before contacting a provider.

There is no universal submission process or technical shortcut that guarantees a business will be recommended. A more practical approach is to strengthen the information available about the company so search and AI systems have enough reliable context to understand what it does, where it operates, and what it is qualified to discuss. If you are weighing how this fits alongside classic rankings, read whether SEO still matters with AI search.

Start With Clarity

One of the first things we would evaluate is whether the website explains the business clearly to someone encountering it for the first time.

A visitor should be able to determine what the company does, which services it provides, who it serves, where it operates, and what differentiates it without having to interpret vague brand language. The same clarity that helps customers also gives search systems better context.

This is particularly important for companies that have expanded over time. A business may have started with one service or one location and gradually added new capabilities, markets, or divisions without updating the website architecture to reflect the change. When that happens, the company may be far more sophisticated than its digital presence suggests.

Establish Geographic Relevance Naturally

For regional businesses, geography often matters. A contractor serving Yakima, Ellensburg, and the Tri-Cities should make those relationships clear, but that does not require repeating city names in every heading and paragraph.

Useful local context can come from service-area information, actual projects, local staff, customer questions, relevant regulations, regional climate considerations, or differences in how services are delivered across markets. Strong local SEO fundamentals support both traditional and AI-driven discovery.

The goal is to make the company's presence in the region easy to understand without creating pages that feel written primarily for an algorithm.

Build a Legitimate Footprint Beyond the Website

A company's own website is only one source of information about the business. Search platforms can also encounter customer reviews, Google Business Profile data, local business organizations, trade associations, industry publications, vendor listings, partnerships, news coverage, and other third-party references.

We generally place more value on a smaller number of credible, relevant mentions than on a large number of low-quality directory listings. A legitimate regional trade association, chamber membership, industry publication, or supplier relationship provides more useful context than a directory created solely for link building.

For local companies, consistency also matters. Business names, locations, services, and other important details should not conflict unnecessarily across major platforms. Consistent brand identity across listings, signage, and digital touchpoints reinforces that clarity.

Publish Material That Adds Something New

As AI makes generic content easier to produce, the value of first-party knowledge increases.

An article titled Five Benefits of Professional Landscaping can be generated by virtually any company. A detailed explanation of what homeowners in Central Washington should consider before selecting irrigation, plants, or landscape materials has the potential to contain far more useful and distinctive information.

The same principle applies across industries. Contractors can explain recurring project challenges. Manufacturers can discuss technical decisions. Law firms can clarify processes they regularly encounter. Healthcare organizations can answer the questions patients repeatedly ask. Agencies can publish findings from experiments, workflows, and actual campaign analysis.

Content becomes more defensible when it originates from experience rather than from a keyword list. That is also what makes a useful organic search strategy durable over time.

Avoid Manufacturing Authority

One of the risks of AI-assisted content production is the temptation to create specificity that is not actually supported by the business.

Statistics, customer stories, project results, certifications, service areas, and claims about local conditions should only appear when they are accurate. A website does not become more authoritative by sounding more certain than the company's real-world experience supports.

We would rather publish a narrower, accurate resource than a highly detailed article built around invented expertise.

Summary

Improving AI visibility is less about finding a technical trick and more about strengthening the company's overall authority and clarity online.

Businesses should make their expertise easy to understand, develop meaningful depth around the subjects that matter, maintain accurate regional information, and earn legitimate recognition outside their own websites. Those practices support AI search, traditional SEO, and the customer research process at the same time.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a business submit itself directly to ChatGPT?

There is no universal submission process that guarantees a company will appear in ChatGPT recommendations.

Does schema markup help with AI search?

Structured data can make certain information easier for search engines to interpret, but it does not replace strong content, clear business information, or broader authority.

Do reviews matter?

Reviews are valuable third-party signals and are especially important for local customers evaluating businesses.

Should companies publish large amounts of AI-generated content?

We would prioritize quality and first-party insight over volume. Publishing more pages is not inherently valuable if the material adds little new information.

title: Zero-Click Search Is Changing Local Marketing in Washington
metaTitle: Zero-Click Search & Local Marketing in Washington
metaDescription: Customers can discover and contact businesses without visiting their websites. Learn how zero-click search is changing local marketing and measurement.
contentHtml:
A customer can discover a business, evaluate it, and make contact without ever appearing as a website visitor.

Consider someone in Richland looking for an HVAC contractor. They search Google, compare companies in the map results, read reviews, view photographs, check hours, and call directly from the listing. The contractor receives a legitimate lead, while Google Analytics records no website session.

This type of behavior is not entirely new. Google Business Profile and map results have supported direct customer actions for years. What is changing is the number of search experiences where customers can gather substantial information before visiting a website.

AI-generated search results make that trend more visible, but the underlying issue has existed in local marketing for some time: traffic and visibility are not always the same thing. For broader context on how search is evolving, see does SEO still matter with AI search.

Local Search Has Always Included Zero-Click Behavior

For many local businesses, the desired outcome of a search is relatively simple.

A restaurant customer may need hours, directions, reviews, and a phone number. A homeowner with an urgent plumbing problem may want to confirm that the company serves the area and then call. A potential legal client may require considerably more information and spend much longer reviewing the firm's website.

The role of the website depends on the purchase.

That is why we are cautious about interpreting a decline or increase in sessions without additional context. A local campaign can generate meaningful business activity that is not fully represented by website traffic alone.

AI Expands the Number of Research Paths

AI search introduces additional ways customers can gather information without clicking through to an individual website.

A person may ask an AI platform to explain a service, compare different approaches, or identify considerations before hiring a provider. They may then search the company name directly, return later through another channel, or contact a business after encountering it multiple times.

Those journeys are more difficult to attribute neatly. That makes AI search visibility and traditional discovery work together rather than compete.

That does not mean attribution should be abandoned. It means businesses and agencies need to evaluate more than a single metric.

Traffic Still Matters

The emergence of zero-click behavior should not become an excuse for ignoring poor website performance.

If a contractor's high-intent organic traffic declines substantially, we want to understand why. If an important service page loses rankings or form submissions decrease, those changes deserve attention.

Website traffic remains especially important for complex services, higher-consideration purchases, and customers who need to compare providers before making contact.

Zero-click measurement should add context to traditional reporting rather than replace it.

A Broader Measurement Framework

For a local business, we would typically want to understand several signals together. Organic impressions can show whether search visibility is increasing. Rankings provide additional context around competitive queries. Google Business Profile actions help measure local interactions. Calls and form submissions show lead activity. Branded searches can indicate growing awareness, while analytics can identify traffic from AI platforms where referral information is available.

Most importantly, these signals should eventually be connected to qualified leads and business results whenever possible.

A campaign that produces more sessions but fewer qualified leads is not necessarily improving. Conversely, a campaign that generates fewer website visits but more calls from high-intent local searches may be performing better than traffic data alone suggests. Strong local SEO and map visibility often drive those calls even when site traffic looks flat.

City-specific service pages also help Google understand where you work. If you serve multiple markets across Washington, see how local SEO supports multi-market visibility.

Summary

The purpose of local marketing is not to maximize sessions in an analytics platform. It is to create meaningful visibility that leads to business.

As customer journeys become more fragmented, measurement needs to reflect that reality. Traffic, rankings, map visibility, calls, forms, branded searches, and emerging AI referral data all provide pieces of the same picture.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a zero-click search?

A zero-click search occurs when the user gets the information or takes an action without visiting a traditional website result.

Can zero-click search generate leads?

Yes. Calls from Google Business Profile are a common example.

Is AI responsible for zero-click behavior?

No. Zero-click search existed before modern AI tools, although AI is expanding the number of situations where customers can receive answers without clicking through.

Should businesses still invest in their websites?

Yes. Websites remain important for search visibility, authority, detailed research, conversions, and customer trust.

title: SEO vs. Google Ads for Pacific Northwest Businesses: Where Should the First Dollar Go?
metaTitle: SEO vs. Google Ads: Where Should You Invest?
metaDescription: Should a Pacific Northwest business invest in SEO or Google Ads first? The answer depends on lead urgency, customer value, competition, and buying behavior.
contentHtml:
The SEO versus Google Ads question is often presented as if one channel should always win. In practice, the better answer depends on how quickly the business needs leads, how customers search, how valuable an average customer is, and how much time the company can afford to spend building visibility.

Because the two channels solve different problems, we generally prefer to begin with the economics and sales process rather than with the marketing tactic.

A New HVAC Company May Need Paid Search First

Consider a new HVAC company serving the Tri-Cities. If the company needs calls immediately, paid search can provide access to existing demand much faster than an organic campaign is likely to.

Heating and cooling services also have clear high-intent searches. When equipment fails during a period of extreme heat or cold, customers may already be looking for a provider. Google Ads management can put a business in front of those customers while organic visibility develops.

That does not mean SEO should be ignored. It means the timing of the two investments may be different.

A Custom Home Builder Has a Different Sales Cycle

A custom home builder is likely to face a longer research process and a much higher-value transaction. Prospective customers may compare portfolios, neighborhoods, project types, design approaches, timelines, and previous work over an extended period.

In that environment, the website itself needs to carry more of the sales process.

Strong project galleries, detailed service pages, location expertise, FAQs, process explanations, and useful content can build authority over time. Paid search may still contribute, but the long-term value of an informative website and strong organic search presence becomes especially important. For what a modern site needs to support that journey, see what a landing page should accomplish.

Niche B2B Companies Can Benefit From Modest Search Volume

Search volume can also be misleading.

A specialized manufacturer in Washington may only have a few hundred relevant searches available each month. That can appear insignificant compared with a consumer category generating tens of thousands of searches.

If one new customer represents substantial lifetime value, however, those few hundred searches may be extremely important.

SEO does not require enormous volume to be valuable. It requires commercially relevant demand.

Sometimes Neither Channel Should Be First

There are also businesses where neither SEO nor paid search deserves the first marketing dollar.

A new restaurant might need stronger Google Maps visibility, reviews, photography, local awareness, social media, or community outreach before investing heavily in long-form search content.

A referral-driven professional service may benefit more from improving reputation, email follow-up, or sales processes.

Good strategy occasionally means rejecting the options presented and choosing another channel entirely. Budget discipline matters too; see why marketing should be treated as an investment.

Why SEO and Paid Search Often Work Better Together

When budget allows, SEO and paid search can provide useful information to one another.

Paid campaigns can reveal which searches generate qualified leads, which services attract demand, which geographic markets perform well, and which landing-page messages convert. Organic strategy can use those findings to prioritize service pages and content.

At the same time, organic visibility can gradually reduce dependence on paid traffic for certain searches and create additional exposure throughout the research process.

The objective is not to prove one channel superior. It is to use each where it has the strongest business case. Timeline expectations for organic growth are covered in what businesses should know about SEO.

Summary

The best answer to SEO versus Google Ads begins with the customer rather than the platform.

Businesses should consider how urgently they need leads, how customers research their services, what a new customer is worth, how competitive the market is, and whether the company already has meaningful organic visibility.

Once those factors are understood, the appropriate balance between paid and organic search becomes much easier to determine.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which works faster, SEO or Google Ads?

Google Ads can generate visibility much faster. SEO generally requires more time to build sustainable rankings and authority.

Which produces a better return?

Either can produce a strong return when the economics are favorable and the campaign is managed well. Customer value and acquisition cost matter more than broad channel averages.

Should a new business use both?

If budget allows, combining immediate paid visibility with a longer-term organic strategy can be effective.

When might SEO not be a priority?

If search demand is limited, the business cannot currently handle more leads, or another channel aligns better with customer behavior, SEO may not deserve the first investment.

title: Local SEO in Washington Is More Than Creating a Page for Every City
metaTitle: Local SEO in Washington: Beyond City Pages
metaDescription: Creating dozens of nearly identical city pages is not a complete local SEO strategy. Learn how Washington businesses can build more useful local content.
contentHtml:
Location pages can be an important part of a local SEO strategy, but creating one page for every city a business serves is not automatically the right approach.

We regularly see websites built around the assumption that more geographic pages must lead to more local visibility. A service page is duplicated, the city name is replaced, and a new URL is added for every market on the list. The result may contain dozens of pages without providing substantially more useful information to customers.

For businesses operating across Washington, a better approach is to consider how geography actually affects the service and the way customers search.

Geography Matters, but Not Every Market Is the Same

A company legitimately serving Yakima and the Tri-Cities may benefit from content focused on both areas. Those markets are meaningful parts of the business and may have distinct search demand.

That does not mean the pages should be identical.

A business serving customers across Central Washington may travel substantial distances between projects, while a contractor operating in the Seattle area may serve a relatively compact geographic region containing many cities and neighborhoods. A statewide B2B company may have one physical location while performing work throughout Washington.

Those operating models should influence how the website is structured.

Local Content Should Support the Service

One of the easiest ways to make a location page unique is to fill it with general information about the city. That may satisfy a superficial uniqueness requirement, but it often does little for the customer.

Someone searching for an electrician in Spokane is not primarily interested in the history of Spokane. They want to know whether the company provides the service they need, whether it works in their area, and whether it appears qualified to handle the project.

Local information should therefore support the service rather than distract from it. For examples of what that looks like in practice, see what makes a good local service page.

Depending on the industry, useful local context might include actual projects, service differences, climate considerations, regional regulations, customer questions, staff serving the area, photographs, and information about how the company operates in the market.

Localization Should Change by Industry

There is no universal template for useful localization.

Climate may be highly relevant to landscaping, roofing, paving, HVAC, and construction. It may be largely irrelevant to a law firm or accounting practice.

A regional contractor may benefit from discussing service logistics and project experience. A healthcare organization may need to focus more on locations, providers, insurance, and access. A professional-services company may need to establish experience serving businesses within a particular regional economy.

The page should reflect what geography actually changes about the customer's decision.

Sometimes Fewer Pages Are Better

There are situations where one strong regional page may be more useful than a collection of thin city pages.

If a company serves ten small communities in the same general area and cannot identify meaningful differences between them, we would at least question whether ten separate URLs provide enough value to justify their existence.

That does not mean fewer pages are always better. It means page count should not be the objective.

A local SEO strategy should reflect the business's actual service areas, customer behavior, search demand, and ability to create useful content. When you evaluate whether the architecture is working, start with what actually matters in an SEO audit rather than page count alone. Broader search shifts are covered in does SEO still matter with AI search.

Summary

Local SEO is not a competition to see how many Washington city names can appear on a website.

The stronger approach is to show customers and search engines that the business genuinely provides a specific service within the markets it serves. That may involve dedicated city pages, regional pages, Google Business Profile optimization, stronger service content, or a combination of all four.

Website architecture should follow the realities of the business rather than a rigid SEO template.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should a business create a page for every city it serves?

Not automatically. Search demand, business importance, geographic relevance, and the ability to provide useful content should all influence the decision.

Can location pages contain similar information?

Yes. The service itself does not change simply because the city changes. The concern is whether the page provides any meaningful additional value.

Should neighborhoods have their own pages?

Only when they reflect how customers actually search and how the business operates.

Should location pages appear in the sitemap?

Canonical, indexable location pages that a business wants search engines to discover should generally be included in the sitemap.

title: How Long Does SEO Take? What We Look for in Months 1, 3, 6, and 12
metaTitle: How Long Does SEO Take? What We Look For
metaDescription: SEO does not follow a fixed timeline. Learn what we typically evaluate during months 1, 3, 6, and 12 of an SEO campaign.
contentHtml:
There is no reliable way to promise that an SEO campaign will produce a specific ranking by a specific date. Websites begin from different levels of authority, industries have different degrees of competition, and individual markets can behave very differently.

What we can do is establish reasonable expectations for the types of signals we want to see as a campaign progresses.

Rather than evaluating SEO through a single keyword or an arbitrary deadline, we prefer to look at the progression from technical foundation to search visibility, traffic, leads, and long-term learning.

Month 1: Establish the Foundation

The first month of an SEO campaign is often less visible than later stages because much of the work involves understanding the website and establishing reliable measurement.

We typically want to confirm that Google Search Console and analytics are configured correctly, important pages are indexable, the sitemap is accurate, redirects and canonical tags make sense, and conversion tracking is functioning. For local businesses, we also want to understand the Google Business Profile, geographic priorities, service areas, and existing local visibility.

Equally important, we need to understand the business. A website can be technically well optimized while targeting services the company has little interest in selling. SEO priorities should reflect revenue goals, service priorities, geographic expansion plans, and the types of customers the business actually wants.

Around Month 3: Look for Evidence That Google Is Responding

By the third month, we generally want to see evidence that the site is moving in the right direction, although that does not mean every target search should be on page one.

Impressions can begin to increase before traffic changes significantly. New pages may start appearing for relevant searches. Existing terms can move from deep in the results toward more competitive positions. Page-two terms may begin approaching page one.

These changes are useful because they can act as leading indicators.

A page moving from position 70 to position 25 may not generate meaningful traffic yet, but the movement tells us that Google is beginning to associate the page with the subject. That can influence what we improve next.

Around Month 6: Evaluate Whether Visibility Is Becoming Opportunity

After several months, we should have enough data to evaluate the campaign more strategically.

We want to understand which pages are gaining visibility, which services are attracting qualified organic users, which markets are responding, and whether rankings are beginning to translate into calls, forms, and other conversions.

This is also when underperforming assumptions become easier to identify. A content category we expected to perform may remain stagnant, while another service or geographic area gains traction much faster than anticipated.

The strategy should respond to those findings rather than continue unchanged simply because the original plan said so. See what actually matters in an SEO audit for how we prioritize those shifts.

Around Month 12: Evaluate What Compounded

A full year of campaign data should produce more than a ranking report.

By this point, we want to understand which parts of the strategy created durable value and what the business learned from the search data.

One service category may have generated significantly more visibility than others. A specific location may have proven much more competitive than expected. An educational topic may have become an important source of discovery. A service page may have performed poorly despite repeated optimization.

Those findings should make the next year of SEO more informed than the first.

Why Timelines Vary So Much

A long-established service business in Yakima with a strong reputation is not starting from the same position as a new company trying to rank throughout Seattle. Neither resembles a niche manufacturer targeting specialized searches nationally.

Competition, domain history, content quality, backlinks, existing brand recognition, technical health, and search demand all influence the timeline.

For that reason, we think it is more useful to establish milestones and leading indicators than to promise an exact result by an exact date. Local architecture choices also affect timing; see local SEO beyond city pages. For how SEO compares to paid search when speed matters, read SEO vs. Google Ads. Search evolution is covered in does SEO still matter with AI search.

Summary

We tend to think about SEO as a progression from foundation to discovery, visibility, traffic, leads, and learning.

The process is not perfectly linear, and individual campaigns can move faster or slower. What matters is whether the evidence suggests that the website is becoming more visible for commercially relevant searches and whether that visibility is contributing to business goals over time.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can SEO work in less than six months?

Yes. Established websites can sometimes respond quickly to strong improvements.

Can SEO take longer than a year?

It can, particularly in highly competitive markets or when a website begins with limited authority.

What is an early sign that SEO is working?

Growth in relevant impressions, indexed pages, and rankings can provide useful early indicators before significant traffic or lead growth occurs.

When should the strategy change?

When search data repeatedly contradicts the assumptions behind the campaign, the strategy should adjust rather than continue unchanged.

title: How Much Should a Local Business Spend on Digital Marketing?
metaTitle: How Much Should a Local Business Spend on Marketing?
metaDescription: Marketing budgets should reflect customer value, margins, growth goals, and capacity. Learn how local businesses can think about digital marketing spend.
contentHtml:
Marketing budget recommendations are often reduced to a percentage of revenue. While those benchmarks can provide general context, they are rarely sufficient for making an actual investment decision.

A residential service company, a commercial contractor, and a specialized manufacturer may all generate similar annual revenue while having completely different margins, customer values, sales cycles, and growth goals. Their marketing budgets should reflect those differences.

We generally prefer to begin with the economics of acquiring a customer.

Customer Value Provides the Necessary Context

Suppose a marketing campaign generates ten leads at a cost of $200 each. Whether those leads are expensive depends entirely on what happens next.

If the ten leads produce two low-margin customers worth only a few hundred dollars each, the economics may not work. If one of those leads becomes a commercial client worth tens of thousands of dollars over the relationship, the same acquisition cost may be extremely attractive.

This is why cost-per-lead benchmarks are not particularly useful without information about close rate, margin, average customer value, and lifetime value.

Marketing decisions become much more rational when the business understands what it can afford to spend to acquire a good customer.

Capacity Should Influence the Budget

A business's ability to handle more work is another important factor.

If a contractor is already booked several months out and cannot hire enough technicians, aggressively increasing lead volume may create operational problems rather than healthy growth.

In that situation, the marketing strategy might shift toward higher-value services, more profitable project types, different geographic markets, recruiting, retention, or customer communication rather than simply increasing lead generation.

Marketing should support the business's current growth constraints instead of operating independently from them.

Pacific Northwest Markets Are Not Interchangeable

Competitive conditions also vary significantly across the region.

The cost of reaching a customer in Seattle may be very different from the cost in Yakima or the Tri-Cities. A rural service-area business can face different geographic challenges than a company operating within a dense metro area. Consumer behavior, competition, media costs, and search demand can all vary by market.

Those differences should be considered when evaluating budget requirements.

A company expanding into a new market may need more investment than one defending an established position in its home market.

Avoid Dividing a Small Budget Across Too Many Channels

One of the most common budgeting mistakes is attempting to participate in every marketing channel without investing enough in any of them to learn what works.

SEO, Google Ads, Meta, LinkedIn, email, video, social media, and display advertising can all be useful in the right situation. They do not all need to be funded simultaneously.

For a business with a limited budget, concentration is often more valuable. Choose the channels that best match customer behavior, invest enough to produce meaningful data, evaluate the results, and expand from there. When choosing between paid and organic search, see SEO vs. Google Ads. Timeline expectations for organic growth are covered in how long SEO takes. Your website also affects how efficiently every channel converts; see what a business website needs to do in 2026.

Summary

The best marketing budget is one that reflects how the business actually makes money.

Companies should understand what a customer is worth, how frequently leads become customers, how aggressively they want to grow, where operational constraints exist, and how competitive their target markets are.

Once those factors are clear, the budget becomes a business decision rather than an arbitrary percentage.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is 10% of revenue a good marketing budget?

It can be appropriate for some companies and completely inappropriate for others. Growth stage, margin, customer value, and competition all matter.

How much should a business spend on Google Ads?

The amount should reflect available demand, customer value, acceptable acquisition cost, and the level of competition in the market.

Should a new business spend more on marketing?

New companies often require more investment because they have less brand recognition, organic visibility, repeat business, and referral activity.

Should marketing spend increase as the company grows?

Not automatically. Investment should reflect growth goals, efficiency, capacity, and the opportunities available in the market.

title: What We Think a Business Website Needs to Do in 2026
metaTitle: What a Business Website Needs to Do in 2026
metaDescription: A modern business website needs to do more than look good. Learn how websites can support sales, search visibility, authority, and customer education.
contentHtml:
Many established business websites still follow the traditional brochure model: a homepage, an about page, a short services page, a gallery, and a contact form.

That structure is not inherently wrong, but it can be insufficient for a company with multiple services, geographic markets, customer types, or complex buying decisions. A website should do more than confirm that the business exists. It should help customers understand the company, support the sales process, establish expertise, and provide search engines with enough context to interpret what the business actually does.

The Website Should Explain the Business Clearly

A strong website should make the company easier to understand than a salesperson has time to explain during an introductory call.

Customers often have recurring questions about services, cost, timing, project scope, geographic availability, qualifications, and what happens after they make contact. Answering those questions online helps prospective customers become better informed before entering the sales process.

That does not reduce the value of human interaction. It improves the quality of the conversation by allowing salespeople to spend more time on the questions that actually require judgment.

Important Services Need Enough Depth

One of the issues we often see is a disconnect between the importance of a service to the business and the amount of information devoted to it on the website.

A service may represent a substantial percentage of company revenue while receiving only a short paragraph on a general services page. That makes it difficult for customers to understand the offering and gives search engines limited context around an important part of the business.

Strategically important services, industries, and markets often deserve enough space to be explained properly. See what makes a good local service page for how geography fits into that structure.

Proof Should Be Built Into the Site

Businesses frequently describe themselves as experienced, trusted, or high quality. Those claims are more persuasive when the website provides evidence.

Depending on the company, that proof may include project galleries, case studies, reviews, certifications, employee expertise, before-and-after examples, client lists, awards, detailed process information, or examples of completed work.

Strong websites do not rely entirely on adjectives. They make it easy for customers to evaluate the underlying evidence.

Search Optimization Should Improve the Site Rather Than Distort It

Search visibility should influence website architecture, subject coverage, metadata, internal linking, and technical implementation. It should not make the site unpleasant to read.

A footer containing dozens of city names, repetitive keyword phrases, or hundreds of nearly identical pages may technically increase the number of search-targeted URLs while reducing the quality of the overall website.

The strongest SEO work generally makes the site clearer and more complete. Broader search shifts are covered in does SEO still matter with AI search.

Maintainability Matters After Launch

A website is not finished when it goes live.

Someone still needs to update staff information, publish content, adjust services, replace photographs, change contact information, add projects, and respond to changes in the business.

The technology used to build the site should therefore reflect who will manage it afterward. A visually impressive website that requires a developer for routine updates can become outdated quickly if the organization does not have the resources to maintain it. If you are weighing a full replacement, read should you rebuild your website.

The Website Is Becoming a Knowledge Source

AI-driven search makes comprehensive business information increasingly valuable.

A website should contain the best available explanation of the company's services, expertise, markets, people, and perspective. That information helps customers, traditional search engines, and AI systems understand what the company is qualified to discuss.

This does not require turning every website into a massive publication. It does mean treating website content strategy as part of the core architecture rather than as an afterthought. Professional website design should support both goals.

Summary

A successful website project should not be defined simply by whether the new site looks better than the old one.

The more useful question is whether the website provides a stronger digital representation of the company. Design matters, but so do search visibility, customer education, proof, conversion, maintainability, and the ability to support future growth.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many pages should a business website have?

There is no ideal number. The site should contain enough information to represent the business accurately and help customers make decisions.

Does every service need its own page?

Not always, but strategically important services often benefit from dedicated content.

Should every business have a blog?

Only if the company has useful information to publish and a reason to maintain it consistently.

Should websites be designed specifically for AI search?

Websites should primarily serve customers, but important business information should also be clearly structured and accessible to search systems.

title: Should You Rebuild Your Website? What We Evaluate Before Recommending It
metaTitle: Should You Rebuild Your Website? | YB Marketing
metaDescription: Not every older website needs replacing. Learn what we evaluate before recommending that a business invest in a full website rebuild.
contentHtml:
A company that builds websites has an obvious incentive to recommend a new website whenever a client is unhappy with the current one. We do not think that should be the default answer.

There are situations where a rebuild is clearly justified. There are also situations where replacing the existing site introduces unnecessary cost, complexity, and SEO risk when a more limited improvement would solve the actual problem.

Before recommending a rebuild, we would want to understand what is wrong with the current site and what the business stands to gain by replacing it.

Is the Technology Actually Holding the Business Back?

An older website is not automatically a bad website.

If the platform is secure, maintainable, reasonably fast, and easy for the team to update, its age alone may not justify a rebuild. On the other hand, a site dependent on outdated plugins, unsupported custom code, or a difficult content-management process can create ongoing technical debt.

The important question is whether the technology is creating real operational or marketing limitations.

What Organic Visibility Already Exists?

Search performance deserves particular attention before a rebuild.

A website can look outdated while still ranking very well. If that site is generating meaningful organic traffic, leads, backlinks, and brand visibility, replacing it without understanding those assets creates unnecessary risk.

Before changing the structure, we would want to identify which pages rank, which URLs receive traffic, which pages have valuable backlinks, what Google currently has indexed, and which areas of the site contribute to conversions.

That information should influence the new architecture and redirect plan. See what actually matters in an SEO audit for how we prioritize those findings and protecting organic visibility during migration.

Has the Business Outgrown the Existing Structure?

A website rebuild becomes more compelling when the company itself has changed substantially.

A business may have expanded from one market to several. It may have added service divisions, changed its ideal customer, acquired another company, entered new industries, or developed capabilities that the current website barely mentions.

In those cases, the challenge is larger than visual design. The site no longer represents the business accurately.

A new architecture can provide an opportunity to align the website with what the company has become. For what the new site should accomplish, see what a business website needs to do in 2026.

Is the Website Creating Friction for Customers?

Usability problems can also justify more substantial changes.

Important information may be difficult to find on mobile devices. Forms may be unreliable. Navigation may reflect an old organizational structure. The contact path may be unclear. The website may use vague messaging that requires insider knowledge to understand.

These issues affect the customer experience directly and can influence conversion performance.

Can the Team Maintain the Website?

Post-launch workflow should also be considered.

If every routine content change requires outside development support, the website may become stale simply because updating it is inconvenient. A company that publishes frequently may need a very different administrative experience than one that changes content only a few times each year.

Technology should reflect the way the organization actually plans to use the site. A thoughtful website redesign accounts for that from the start.

When We Would Consider Keeping the Existing Site

If a website ranks well, converts well, remains technically stable, accurately represents the business, and is easy to maintain, a full rebuild may not be necessary.

Leadership may simply dislike the visual presentation. In that case, targeted design, usability, or conversion improvements could provide a better return than replacing the entire site.

Starting over is not automatically the same thing as improving. Realistic SEO timelines are covered in how long SEO takes.

Summary

A website rebuild should solve identifiable business problems.

Before recommending one, we want to understand what the current site does well, where it creates friction, what can be preserved, and what the organization needs the new website to accomplish.

The objective is not simply to launch something newer. It is to create a better-performing business asset. If you want to discuss a website project, we are happy to review the current site first.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can rebuilding a website hurt SEO?

Yes. Removing content, changing URLs, altering internal links, or mishandling redirects can cause organic visibility to decline.

Should existing URLs be preserved?

When a URL performs well and still fits the new architecture, preserving it can reduce migration risk.

How should SEO be protected during a rebuild?

Existing URLs, rankings, traffic, backlinks, and conversions should be reviewed before launch. Redirects, metadata, technical SEO, and indexing should then be validated during the migration.

Should a business rebuild simply because the site looks old?

Not necessarily. Visual improvements can sometimes be made without replacing the entire website.

title: What Makes a Good Local Service Page? Examples From Washington Businesses
metaTitle: What Makes a Good Local Service Page for SEO?
metaDescription: Learn how Washington businesses can create useful local service pages that reflect real geography, customer needs, and regional expertise.
contentHtml:
A strong local service page should make two things clear: the company provides the service the customer needs, and the company genuinely serves the market where that customer is located.

Many location pages accomplish those goals only superficially. They repeat a city name throughout otherwise generic copy without adding information that helps the customer understand the business or the service.

Useful localization should be more substantive than that, and the appropriate approach changes significantly by industry.

HVAC in the Tri-Cities

For an HVAC company serving Kennewick, Pasco, and Richland, the primary subject of the page should still be heating and cooling services.

Regional context can strengthen the page when it is relevant. Seasonality, equipment considerations, service coverage, common customer questions, and the company's experience working throughout the Tri-Cities can all help establish legitimate geographic relevance.

What does not help is adding unrelated local history simply to make the page appear unique.

Roofing in Western Washington

A roofing company serving the Seattle area has a different opportunity.

Regional weather can have a meaningful relationship to roofing materials, maintenance, inspections, drainage, and common repair issues. Housing and commercial building characteristics may also influence how services are presented.

Actual project photography, service-area information, and local examples can provide stronger evidence of regional experience than repeatedly using the phrase Seattle roofing contractor.

Landscaping in Central Washington

Localization may play an even larger role for landscaping.

Climate, irrigation, water use, plant selection, seasonal maintenance, and soil conditions can all shape the recommendations a landscaping company makes. A business operating in Central Washington has an opportunity to demonstrate expertise by explaining how those factors influence its work.

That is substantially more useful than simply stating that the company provides landscaping in Yakima.

Professional Services Require Different Localization

The same approach should not be applied mechanically to every industry.

Climate may be highly relevant to landscaping, HVAC, roofing, and paving but almost irrelevant to a law firm. A professional-services company may instead establish local relevance through market knowledge, jurisdictions, offices, team experience, customer types, or the communities it serves.

Localization should reflect the actual service rather than follow a predetermined checklist.

Templates Provide Structure, Not Substance

A useful local-page framework might include an introduction to the service, detailed service information, process, proof, geographic coverage, FAQs, and a call to action.

That framework can improve consistency across a website. Strong site architecture makes those pages easier to navigate and maintain.

The substance inside the framework still needs to come from the business. Without real project information, service differences, customer questions, or regional knowledge, the site risks creating a collection of visually polished duplicate pages. For when fewer pages may be better, see local SEO beyond city pages. Prioritization guidance is in what actually matters in an SEO audit. Modern site requirements are covered in what a business website needs in 2026. A solid local SEO foundation supports all of it.

Summary

A strong local service page does not need to remind the reader of the city name in every section.

It needs to establish that the company understands the service, genuinely operates in the market, and has enough relevant expertise to be considered by the customer.

That is a more useful standard for local content than keyword repetition or artificial uniqueness.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should every local page be completely different?

No. Core service information will naturally overlap. The goal is meaningful differentiation where geography actually matters.

How much local information should be included?

Enough to establish legitimate regional relevance without distracting from the service itself.

Can surrounding cities be mentioned?

Yes, when they genuinely fall within the company's service area.

Are local project photos useful?

Real project photography can provide strong evidence of both experience and geographic presence.

title: Why We Started Building Our Own Marketing Tools at YB
metaTitle: Why We're Building Our Own Marketing Tools | YB
metaDescription: We did not need another marketing dashboard. We needed better ways to connect client data, priorities, and workflows into useful decisions.
contentHtml:
Marketing agencies do not have a shortage of software. In many cases, the challenge is the opposite.

A single SEO campaign can involve Google Analytics, Google Search Console, rank-tracking software, call tracking, project-management tools, CRM data, website information, and internal client notes. Each system may provide useful information, but the marketer still has to connect those sources and determine what they actually mean for the client.

That is what led us to start building more of our own internal tools.

The objective was not to create another dashboard. It was to get closer to answering a more valuable question: What should we pay attention to next?

The Problem Is Often Interpretation, Not Access to Data

We already have platforms that can display rankings, traffic, calls, impressions, and conversions.

The more difficult work is identifying relationships between those signals.

A service page might be gaining impressions but remain stuck just outside page one. An older article may still generate substantial visibility while gradually losing clicks. A geographic market may be showing unexpected growth. A service the client considers strategically important may have almost no organic presence.

Those are not simply reporting observations. They are potential work priorities. That is the same lens we use in what actually matters in an SEO audit.

Client Context Changes the Meaning of the Data

Marketing data is only useful when it is interpreted in the context of the business.

A keyword can have excellent search volume while representing work the client no longer wants. A city may appear attractive from a search perspective while falling outside the company's actual service area. A content recommendation may look logical until it conflicts with regulatory, legal, or brand restrictions.

That is why our internal systems increasingly incorporate information about the client itself: services, geographic priorities, business goals, competitors, existing content, approved terminology, and other constraints.

Better context creates better analysis.

Where We Think AI Is Most Useful

AI can generate large amounts of content quickly, but that is not the application we find most interesting.

We are more interested in using AI to review information that would otherwise require substantial manual analysis. That can include comparing time periods, surfacing anomalies, identifying content gaps, reviewing search-query patterns, organizing large data sets, and highlighting areas that deserve a strategist's attention.

The human still determines what should be done. The system makes it easier to identify where judgment is needed. That connects to our broader thinking on AI search visibility, does SEO still matter with AI search, and how to show up in AI search.

Testing Internally Before Making Claims

There is a meaningful difference between adding AI to a services page and building it into actual operating processes.

We prefer to test these systems within our own agency first. That allows us to understand where automation helps, where it creates poor recommendations, what types of context improve the output, and where human review remains essential.

Some experiments become useful workflows. Others do not.

That process is valuable because it replaces assumptions with practical experience.

The Goal Is Better Use of Human Attention

We are not trying to remove marketers from the process.

We are trying to reduce the time they spend collecting information that already exists so they can spend more time interpreting it.

If a strategist spends less time manually assembling reports and more time understanding why a page gained visibility, why a service is underperforming, or where a client has a meaningful growth opportunity, the system is doing something useful.

Summary

We are building internal tools because we have encountered specific operational problems that off-the-shelf platforms do not always solve in the way our team needs.

The central question is simple: once all of the data has been collected, how do we make it easier to determine what matters?

That is the problem we think is worth continuing to work on. If you want to talk with our team about a similar challenge, we are happy to start there.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is YB using AI in marketing?

Yes. We are exploring applications involving analysis, reporting, research, workflows, and other areas where AI can support our team.

Does AI write all of YB's content?

No. AI can assist with parts of the process, but useful content still requires business context, accurate source information, and editorial judgment.

Is the goal to replace marketing employees?

No. The primary objective is to reduce repetitive work and improve the information available to the team.

Can similar systems be built for clients?

When a client has a workflow or data problem that can be meaningfully improved through automation or custom development, it may be worth exploring.

title: Why an SEO Score Is Not the Same Thing as an SEO Strategy
metaTitle: What Actually Matters in an SEO Audit? | YB Marketing
metaDescription: A high SEO audit score does not mean a site is performing well. Learn how we prioritize indexing, search opportunities, content, and business impact.
contentHtml:
SEO auditing platforms can be extremely useful. They can identify technical errors, missing metadata, broken links, crawl issues, image problems, and many other conditions that deserve attention.

The mistake is assuming that improving the software's score is the same thing as improving the business's search performance.

A website can achieve an excellent technical score while remaining almost invisible for the services that matter most. Another website can have a long list of minor technical warnings while generating substantial organic leads.

The purpose of an SEO audit should therefore be prioritization rather than perfection.

Not Every Warning Has the Same Business Impact

Consider two potential issues.

The first is a collection of images that need better alt text. The second is a high-margin service page sitting just outside the first page of Google while generating thousands of impressions.

Both may deserve attention, but they do not necessarily deserve equal priority.

SEO teams have limited time and budgets. The audit should help determine which work is most likely to improve visibility, usability, or conversions rather than simply identifying the largest number of errors.

Technical Fundamentals Still Come First

There are technical issues that can affect the entire site and deserve immediate attention.

We want to know whether Google can crawl important pages, whether those pages are indexable, whether canonical tags are appropriate, whether redirects work correctly, and whether the sitemap accurately reflects the site.

Website rebuilds deserve particular attention because migrations can unintentionally remove high-performing URLs, change internal-link structures, or introduce indexing problems. See should you rebuild your website before making major structural changes.

Search Console Often Reveals Better Opportunities

Google Search Console provides a different kind of information because it shows how Google is actually interacting with the website.

A service page appearing frequently in positions 11 through 15 may represent a meaningful opportunity. A page with rapidly increasing impressions may deserve additional support. An older article losing visibility can indicate a need for an update or consolidation. A strategically important service with virtually no search presence can expose a major content gap.

Those observations can influence the work far more directly than a generic list of technical warnings.

Sometimes the Problem Is the Content Structure

SEO issues are not always page-level problems.

A website may have dozens of useful articles around a particular subject but no strong primary page connecting them. Another site may contain a large collection of thin location pages competing with one another. Several older articles may cover essentially the same query and divide authority unnecessarily.

In those situations, the solution may involve creating a stronger content hub, improving internal linking, consolidating overlapping pages, or restructuring an entire section. See local SEO beyond city pages for one common architecture question.

Sometimes the Right Move Is to Remove Content

Websites accumulate content over time.

Old campaign landing pages, outdated services, thin blog posts, duplicate location pages, obsolete announcements, and abandoned content experiments can remain indexed for years.

Adding more content to that environment may increase complexity without improving authority.

In some cases, consolidation, redirection, or removal can create a clearer and more useful website. Those decisions should be made carefully, particularly when an old page still has rankings, traffic, or backlinks.

Business Priorities Should Influence SEO Priorities

This is one of the areas where automated audit tools have natural limitations.

Software can identify search volume. It does not necessarily know which service produces the best margin, which project type the company wants more of, which region is a strategic priority, or which category of customer the sales team no longer wants to pursue.

A successful SEO strategy needs that context. The goal should not be maximum traffic at any cost. It should be greater visibility for searches that support the business.

AI Search Does Not Change That Principle

We are beginning to evaluate websites through the additional lens of AI-driven search. That includes whether the business is clearly represented, whether the site establishes enough depth around important subjects, and whether authoritative information exists that search systems can understand and reference.

The same prioritization principle still applies. We are less interested in completing every item on an AI SEO checklist than in determining whether the work makes the company's expertise clearer, more credible, and easier to discover. Related reading: does SEO still matter with AI search, AI search visibility, how long SEO takes, and website rebuild considerations.

Summary

A useful SEO audit should not end with a spreadsheet containing hundreds of warnings and no indication of what should happen next.

It should identify the issues and opportunities that matter most, explain why they matter, and establish a logical order for addressing them.

Finding problems is relatively easy. Determining which problems are worth solving first is where the strategy begins.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a good SEO score?

There is no universal third-party score that determines whether a website will rank well. Different platforms use different scoring systems.

Should every technical SEO error be fixed?

Legitimate errors should be evaluated, but priority should reflect their likely impact on search performance, usability, and the business.

What do you look at first during an SEO audit?

Crawlability, indexing, site architecture, analytics, Search Console data, important services, existing rankings, technical health, and conversion tracking are common starting points.

Can deleting pages improve SEO?

Consolidating or removing low-value content can sometimes improve the structure and focus of a site. Existing traffic, rankings, and backlinks should be reviewed before making those decisions.

Does an SEO audit now need to include AI search?

We increasingly consider how clearly a site establishes its expertise, topics, entities, and authority alongside traditional search performance.
